inlines.value: As your codebase grows, organizing it into multiple subprojects becomes essential for maintainability, performance, and reuse. Gradle supports this with multi-project builds.

While some small projects and monolithic applications may contain a single build file and source tree, it is often more common for a project to have been split into smaller, interdependent modules. The word "interdependent" is vital, as you typically want to link the many modules together through a single build.

There’s no reason that any of the subprojects in a multi-project build couldn’t themselves be composite builds. This allows teams to independently develop and test build logic or components, then include them in a larger build as needed. For example:

│   ├── settings.gradle(.kts)
│   ├── client
│   │   └── build.gradle(.kts)
│   └── server
│       └── build.gradle(.kts)
├── project-2

├── settings.gradle(.kts)
    ├── app-plugin
    │   └── build.gradle(.kts)
    ├── client-plugin
    │   └── build.gradle(.kts)
    └── server-plugin
        └── build.gradle(.kts)
In this setup, a team could work on
as an entirely independent build. Once their changes are complete, another team could test and validate those changes by integrating `project-3’s changes into the full root build.
